name: Report failed executions to an HTTP endpoint with an error trigger

parameters.content:
## Report failed executions to an HTTP endpoint with an error trigger

## Who's it for

Anyone running scheduled or webhook-driven workflows in production who currently finds out about failures by noticing that nothing happened.

## How it works

n8n lets every workflow nominate an error workflow. When a run fails, that workflow is started with a payload describing the failure. This template receives it with an Error Trigger and posts five fields to an HTTP endpoint of your choice: the workflow name and id, a direct link to the failed execution, the error message, and the name of the node that failed. The execution URL is the part that matters most, because it takes you straight to the run that broke rather than to a list of runs.

## How to set up

1. Import this workflow and save it.
2. Point **Post failure report** at your own endpoint - a Slack or Discord incoming webhook, an internal alerting API, or anything that accepts JSON.
3. Attach a Header Auth credential if your endpoint needs one.
4. In every workflow you want covered, open **Settings > Error workflow** and select this one.

## Requirements

An endpoint that accepts a JSON POST. No paid service is needed.

## How to customize

Swap the HTTP node for the Slack, Telegram, or email node if you prefer a native integration. Add an IF node before it to stay quiet for workflows you do not care about.

## One caveat worth knowing

An error workflow only fires on a thrown error. A run that finishes green while writing nothing never triggers it - for that case add an explicit item-count check and a **Stop and Error** node at the end of the workflow you are protecting.

### 1. Catches any workflow you attach it to
The Error Trigger fires when a workflow that names this one as its error workflow fails. You do not wire it into anything - you select it in **Settings > Error workflow** on each workflow you want covered.

### 2. Sends the five fields worth having
Workflow name and id, the execution URL, the error message, and the node that failed. That combination is enough to open the failed run directly, without going hunting in the executions list.
